items.question: What does a consent management platform do?

items.question: Can we use one checkbox for marketing, analytics and service messages?
items.answer: No. Bundling purposes into one choice makes consent neither specific nor free. Service messages needed to deliver what the customer asked for may rely on a legitimate use instead of consent.

items.question: How do other systems know a customer withdrew consent?
items.answer: Sentinel DPDP sends the change to connected systems through APIs and webhooks, and those systems can also look up consent status before they use the data.

items.question: Can we keep data after an erasure request?
items.answer: Only where retention is required by law, for example tax or banking records. Data kept for internal analytics does not qualify and must be erased.

items.question: Can someone else make a request on a customer's behalf?
items.answer: Yes, a nominee appointed under Section 14 can exercise the Data Principal's rights in the event of death or incapacity, and a parent or lawful guardian acts for a child or a person with disability.

items.question: What happens if we ignore requests?
items.answer: The Data Principal can complain to the Data Protection Board after using your grievance mechanism. Breach of obligations not covered by a specific penalty can attract a penalty of up to ₹50 crore.

layout.heading: Your obligations depend on *your role*
layout.subheading: The DPDP Act assigns different duties to the organisations that decide why data is processed, those that process it for others, and those that help people manage consent.

items.title: Data Fiduciary
items.text: Decides the purpose and means of processing (Section 2(i)). Carries the main obligations: notice, consent or legitimate use, accuracy, security, breach notification, erasure, a contact person and grievance redressal (Sections 4 to 8).

items.title: Data Processor
items.text: Processes personal data on behalf of a Data Fiduciary (Section 2(k)). Has no direct obligations in the Act; it is bound through a valid contract, and the Data Fiduciary remains responsible for its work (Section 8(1) and 8(2)).

items.title: Significant Data Fiduciary
items.text: A Data Fiduciary notified by the Government based on volume and sensitivity of data and risk (Section 10). Must appoint a Data Protection Officer based in India, an independent data auditor, and carry out an annual DPIA and audit (Rule 13).

items.title: Consent Manager
items.text: A person registered with the Board that lets Data Principals give, manage, review and withdraw consent through an accessible, transparent and interoperable platform (Section 6(7) to 6(9), Rule 4). Accountable to the Data Principal.

items.title: Leadership and board

items.text: Interpret obligations, own notices, contracts and the grievance process.

items.text: Reasonable security safeguards, logging, access control and breach response.

items.title: Marketing and CX
items.text: Purpose-wise consent, campaign suppression and preference centres.

items.title: HR
items.text: Employee notices, employment legitimate uses and retention of staff records.

items.title: Procurement
items.text: Vendor assessments and DPDP clauses in processor contracts.

items.question: Can a company be both a Data Fiduciary and a Data Processor?
items.answer: Yes. A company is a Data Fiduciary for its own customers and employees, and a Data Processor when it processes data for a client under contract.

items.question: Who can be a Data Protection Officer?

meta.title: DPDP Act 2023 Explained: Scope, Obligations, Rights and Penalties
meta.description: A plain-language guide to India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the DPDP Rules, 2025: who it applies to, consent, legitimate uses, obligations, rights, the Board and penalties.

layout.heading: The *Digital Personal Data Protection Act*, 2023 explained
layout.subheading: India's first comprehensive data protection law, passed in August 2023 and made operational by the DPDP Rules, 2025. Here is what it requires, in plain language.

layout.heading: Scope: who and what it covers
layout.intro:
The Act applies to the processing of digital personal data in India, whether collected digitally or collected on paper and digitised later. It also applies to processing outside India if it is connected to offering goods or services to Data Principals in India (Section 3).

It does not apply to personal data processed by an individual for personal or domestic purposes, or to personal data made publicly available by the Data Principal or under a legal obligation.

Personal data means any data about an individual who is identifiable by or in relation to that data. Unlike GDPR, the Act does not create special categories of sensitive data: all personal data gets the same protection, with extra rules for children.

layout.heading: Consent, or a legitimate use
layout.intro: Section 4 allows processing for a lawful purpose only with consent or for a legitimate use listed in Section 7.

items.title: Consent (Section 6)
items.text: Free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, by a clear affirmative action, limited to the data necessary for the purpose, and withdrawable as easily as it was given.

items.title: Legitimate uses (Section 7)
items.text: A specified purpose for which the person voluntarily gave the data and did not object; State functions; legal obligations and court orders; medical emergencies; epidemics and disasters; and employment purposes.

items.title: Give a clear, itemised notice with every request for consent (Section 5, Rule 3)
Obtain valid consent or rely on a listed legitimate use (Sections 6 and 7)
Remain responsible for processing by your processors (Section 8(1))
Engage processors only under a valid contract (Section 8(2))
Keep data complete, accurate and consistent when it is used for decisions (Section 8(3))
Protect data with reasonable security safeguards (Section 8(5), Rule 6)
Notify the Board and affected people of every breach (Section 8(6), Rule 7)
Erase data when consent is withdrawn or the purpose is served (Section 8(7), Rule 8)
Publish the contact of a DPO or responsible person (Section 8(9))
Run an effective grievance redressal mechanism (Section 8(10))
Follow additional rules for children and persons with disability (Section 9)
Access
items.text: A summary of their data, the processing done and who it was shared with (Section 11).

items.title: Correction and erasure
items.text: Correct, complete, update or erase their data (Section 12).

items.title: Grievance redressal
items.text: A readily available way to complain, answered within 90 days (Section 13, Rule 14).

items.title: Nomination
items.text: Nominate someone to exercise their rights on death or incapacity (Section 14).

layout.heading: Extra protection for anyone under 18
layout.intro: Before processing a child's personal data, a Data Fiduciary must obtain verifiable consent of a parent or lawful guardian (Section 9(1), Rule 10). It must not process data in a way likely to harm a child, and must not track, behaviourally monitor or target advertising at children (Section 9(3)). The Rules exempt some classes of Data Fiduciaries and purposes, such as healthcare and education providers, for limited activities.
layout.primaryText: Children are anyone under eighteen.

layout.heading: Higher duties for higher risk
layout.intro: The Government can notify any Data Fiduciary or class as a Significant Data Fiduciary, based on the volume and sensitivity of data, risk to Data Principals, impact on the sovereignty and integrity of India, electoral democracy, state security and public order (Section 10). An SDF must appoint a Data Protection Officer based in India, appoint an independent data auditor, and carry out a DPIA and audit every twelve months (Rule 13). The Rules also allow restrictions on transferring specified data outside India for SDFs.
layout.primaryText: Penalty up to ₹150 crore for breach of SDF obligations.

layout.heading: Cross-border transfers and exemptions
layout.intro:
Personal data can be transferred outside India except to countries the Government restricts by notification (Section 16). Stricter sector rules, such as RBI data storage directions, continue to apply.

Section 17 exempts certain processing from most obligations, including processing to enforce legal rights, by courts and tribunals, to prevent or investigate offences, in mergers and schemes approved by a court, and for research, archiving or statistics where the data is not used for decisions about a specific person.

layout.heading: The Data Protection Board of India
layout.intro: The Board is an independent, digital-first body that inquires into breaches and complaints, directs remedies and imposes penalties (Sections 18 to 28). A Data Principal must first use the Data Fiduciary's grievance mechanism. Appeals against the Board's orders go to the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal within sixty days (Section 29). The Board can also accept a voluntary undertaking from a Data Fiduciary (Section 32).
layout.primaryText: The Board was constituted when the Rules were notified.

items.title: Up to ₹250 crore
items.text: Failure to take reasonable security safeguards to prevent a personal data breach (Section 8(5)).

items.title: Up to ₹200 crore
items.text: Failure to notify the Board or affected Data Principals of a breach (Section 8(6)).

items.title: Up to ₹200 crore
items.text: Breach of the additional obligations for children's data (Section 9).

items.title: Up to ₹150 crore
items.text: Breach of the additional obligations of a Significant Data Fiduciary (Section 10).

items.title: Up to ₹50 crore
items.text: Breach of any other provision of the Act or Rules.

items.title: Up to ₹10,000
items.text: Breach of the duties of a Data Principal, such as a false or frivolous complaint (Section 15).

items.title: November 2025: Rules notified
items.text: The Data Protection Board is constituted and its provisions apply immediately.

items.title: November 2026: Consent Managers
items.text: Consent Managers can register with the Board and operate (Rule 4).

items.title: May 2027: Full obligations
items.text: Notice, consent, rights, security, breach, retention, children and SDF obligations apply, and penalties can be imposed.

items.question: Does the DPDP Act apply to small businesses?
items.answer: Yes. There is no size threshold. The Government can exempt certain classes of Data Fiduciaries, including startups, from some provisions by notification, but the core duties apply to all.

items.question: Does it apply to data on paper?
items.answer: Only once it is digitised. Personal data collected on paper and later entered into a system is covered from that point.

items.question: Do individuals get compensation?
items.answer: No. Penalties under the Act go to the Government. The Act does not provide compensation to affected individuals, unlike GDPR.

items.question: Is this legal advice?
items.answer: No. This page summarises the Act and Rules for general understanding. Consult your legal counsel for advice on your situation.

meta.description: How India's DPDP Act, 2023 compares with the EU GDPR: scope, legal bases, sensitive data, children, breach notification, rights, cross-border transfers and penalties.

layout.heading: *DPDP* vs GDPR: what changes for India
layout.subheading: If you have a GDPR programme, much of it carries over. These are the differences that matter.

items.title: Consent that is specific, informed and withdrawable
Rights to access, correction and erasure
Controller and processor (Fiduciary and Processor) roles

layout.heading: What is new or stricter in India

items.title: Grounds for processing
items.text: GDPR has six legal bases including legitimate interests. DPDP has consent and a closed list of legitimate uses, with no general legitimate interests ground.

items.title: Sensitive data
items.text: GDPR has special categories. DPDP treats all personal data alike, with extra rules for children.

items.title: Children
items.text: GDPR lets member states set an age between 13 and 16. DPDP covers everyone under 18, with verifiable parental consent and a ban on tracking and targeted ads.

items.title: Breach notification
items.text: GDPR notifies the authority within 72 hours when there is a risk. DPDP requires notice of every breach to the Board and to each affected person, with no risk threshold.

items.title: Scope
items.text: GDPR covers all personal data. DPDP covers digital personal data, and excludes data made public by the person.

items.title: Rights
items.text: DPDP adds the right to nominate, but has no data portability right and no right against automated decisions.

items.title: Consent Managers
items.text: A new class of registered intermediaries that let people manage consent across fiduciaries. GDPR has no equivalent.

items.title: Penalties
items.text: GDPR fines reach 4% of global turnover and individuals can claim compensation. DPDP sets fixed caps up to ₹250 crore per instance, with no compensation to individuals.

items.title: Cross-border transfers
items.text: GDPR needs adequacy or safeguards. DPDP allows transfers except to countries the Government restricts.

layout.heading: The *DPDP compliance* checklist
layout.subheading: Twenty steps, in the order most organisations take them, to be ready before the full obligations apply in May 2027.

items.title: 1. Appoint an owner and, if needed, a Data Protection Officer
2. Form a cross-functional privacy working group
3. Run a gap assessment against the Act and Rules
4. Agree a roadmap and budget with leadership
5. Inventory personal data across systems, files and vendors
6. Record each processing activity and its purpose
7. Choose a ground for each: consent or a Section 7 use
8. Set a retention period for each data category
9. Write standalone, itemised notices in the languages you need
10. Unbundle consent by purpose on every channel
11. Make withdrawal as easy as giving consent
12. Send notices to customers whose consent predates the Act
13. Publish how to exercise rights and contact your DPO
14. Build a request workflow with identity verification
15. Set up grievance redressal with a 90-day limit
16. Apply reasonable security safeguards and keep logs for a year
17. Prepare a breach playbook with 72-hour Board reporting
18. Assess vendors and add DPDP clauses to contracts
19. Add age checks, parental consent and no tracking for children
20. Train staff and review the programme every year

meta.description: Plain-language definitions of the key terms in India's DPDP Act, 2023 and DPDP Rules, 2025, with section references.

layout.heading: DPDP *glossary*
layout.subheading: The terms you will meet in the Act, the Rules and compliance conversations, defined in plain language with their source.

items.question: Data Principal
items.answer: The individual to whom the personal data relates. For a child it includes the parent or lawful guardian, and for a person with disability, their lawful guardian (Section 2(j)).

items.question: Data Fiduciary
items.answer: Any person who alone or with others determines the purpose and means of processing personal data (Section 2(i)).

items.question: Data Processor
items.answer: Any person who processes personal data on behalf of a Data Fiduciary (Section 2(k)).

items.question: Significant Data Fiduciary (SDF)
items.answer: A Data Fiduciary or class notified by the Government under Section 10, with additional obligations.

items.question: Consent Manager
items.answer: A person registered with the Board who acts as a single point of contact for a Data Principal to give, manage, review and withdraw consent (Section 2(g)).

items.question: Personal data
items.answer: Any data about an individual who is identifiable by or in relation to that data (Section 2(t)).

items.question: Digital personal data
items.answer: Personal data in digital form (Section 2(n)).

items.question: Processing
items.answer: A wholly or partly automated operation on digital personal data, including collection, recording, storage, use, sharing, disclosure, erasure and destruction (Section 2(x)).

items.question: Personal data breach
items.answer: Any unauthorised processing, or accidental disclosure, acquisition, sharing, use, alteration, destruction or loss of access, that compromises the confidentiality, integrity or availability of personal data (Section 2(u)).

items.question: Consent
items.answer: A free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous indication of the Data Principal's wishes, by a clear affirmative action (Section 6(1)).

items.question: Notice
items.answer: Information given with or before a request for consent, describing the data, the purpose and how to exercise rights and complain (Section 5).

items.question: Legitimate use
items.answer: A purpose listed in Section 7 for which personal data may be processed without consent.

items.question: Child
items.answer: An individual who has not completed eighteen years of age (Section 2(f)).

items.question: Verifiable parental consent
items.answer: Consent of a parent or lawful guardian, verified as coming from an identifiable adult (Rule 10).

items.question: Data Protection Officer (DPO)
items.answer: An individual appointed by a Significant Data Fiduciary, based in India and responsible to its board (Section 10(2)).

items.question: Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)
items.answer: A process describing the rights of Data Principals and the purpose of processing, and assessing and managing the risks to them (Section 10(2)(c)).

items.question: Data Protection Board of India
items.answer: The independent body that inquires into breaches and complaints and imposes penalties (Section 18).

items.question: Nomination
items.answer: The right of a Data Principal to nominate another person to exercise their rights on death or incapacity (Section 14).

items.question: Voluntary undertaking
items.answer: A commitment by a Data Fiduciary, accepted by the Board, to take or refrain from an action, which can bar proceedings on that matter (Section 32).

items.question: RoPA
items.answer: Record of Processing Activities: a register of what personal data is processed, why, on what ground and with whom. Not a defined term in the Act, but the practical basis for many obligations.

layout.heading: DPDP questions, *answered*
layout.subheading: Practical answers to the questions we hear most from marketing, legal, IT and leadership teams.

items.question: Does DPDP apply only to paying customers?
items.answer: No. It covers every individual whose digital personal data you process: customers, leads, website visitors, employees, candidates, vendor contacts and more.

items.question: When a user fills a form, can we use the data for anything?
items.answer: No. You may use it for the purpose they gave it for. Using it for something else, such as marketing, needs a notice and separate consent.

items.question: Can we keep using customer data collected over many years?
items.answer: You may continue to process data collected with consent before the Act, but you must send those customers a notice as soon as reasonably practicable, and stop if they withdraw (Section 5(2)).

items.question: If a customer withdraws marketing consent, can we still send transactional messages?
items.answer: Yes. Order, billing and service messages needed for what the customer asked for rely on that request, not on marketing consent.

items.question: Is a privacy policy on our website enough?
items.answer: No. A privacy policy is useful, but the Act requires a specific notice with each request for consent, itemising the data and purposes.

items.question: If a customer asks what data we hold, what must we provide?
items.answer: A summary of their personal data and the processing done on it, the identities of other Data Fiduciaries and Processors it was shared with and what was shared, and other information the Rules specify (Section 11).

items.question: Can we retain data for analytics after an erasure request?
items.answer: No, unless retention is required by law. Internal analytics is not a legal requirement. Anonymised, aggregate data that no longer identifies anyone is outside the Act.

items.question: How fast must we answer complaints?
items.answer: Within the period you publish, which may not exceed 90 days (Rule 14). The customer can go to the Board only after using your mechanism.

items.question: If we have a breach, what exactly must we do?
items.answer: Contain it, then inform each affected Data Principal without delay, and inform the Board without delay with a detailed report within 72 hours (Rule 7).

items.question: Are we responsible for a breach at our vendor?
items.answer: Yes. The Data Fiduciary is responsible for processing done on its behalf (Section 8(1)). Contracts should require vendors to report breaches immediately.

items.question: Can we transfer data to vendors outside India?
items.answer: Yes, unless the Government restricts transfers to that country (Section 16). Sector rules, such as RBI's, may be stricter.

items.question: Do all companies need a DPO?
items.answer: Only Significant Data Fiduciaries must appoint a Data Protection Officer. Every other Data Fiduciary must publish the contact of a person who can answer questions about its processing.

items.question: Can we manage DPDP manually without a platform?
items.answer: A small business with few systems can. Once data flows through several channels and tools, keeping consent in sync and proving it manually becomes impractical.

items.question: What is the deadline?
items.answer: Most obligations apply from May 2027. Consent Manager provisions applied from November 2026.
